newsitem.title: USA: Florida freezes home insurance rates.
newsitem.headline: Florida freezes home insurance rates.

text.p: Florida's insurance commissioner said Friday that homeowners insurance rates will be frozen until he is satisfied private insurers are passing recently enacted state discounts on to consumers.

Reacting to steady increases in homeowners insurance premiums, Florida Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson also warned that companies that do not undertake their "fair share" of homeowners' policies may lose access to more lucrative markets such as automobile and business insurance.
Nelson planned to approach state lawmakers in March with legislation.
"The message is this," Nelson said. " If you want to insure our lives and health...then you're going to have to insure our homes."

Nelson and U.S. insurance companies have wrangled for the past few years over the availability of homeowners insurance in the wake of Hurricane Andrew, which caused nearly $16 billion in claims when it hit South Florida in 1992.
Since that time, many private insurers have stopped issuing new policies and a state-run insurance pool now boasts more than 700,000 policy holders.

Earlier this month, Nelson denied a request from the state-run joint underwriting association for a 5.3 percent increase in homeowners policies that include rate rises of more than 50 percent for some coastal areas.
"There has been this constant mantra that they don't let up, saying rate hike, rate hike, rate hike," Nelson said. "Well, in a word, we've had enough."

Nelson wants the industry to show that discounts passed since 1994 are being passed to consumers. Since 1994, Florida lawmakers have enacted discounts for item such as hurricane- proof shutters, strict building codes and higher deductibles.

He said he will approach state lawmakers this spring to pass a package of insurance reform that would require that companies take "their fair share" of homeowners policies. Insurers countered that, forcing companies to write homeowners insurance along with other products could prompt some companies to pull out of the market altogether.

"You've got a situation with the homeowners market being tight," said Patty Nates, spokeswoman for State Farm Insurance Cos., Florida's largest private insurer with one million policy holders. "Why then extend that to the auto market."
